terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to see the shelf count and the catalogue worked out.

tasks.title: Count every candle on the shelf
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/object-loops.js`, make `totalStock(shelf)` return how many candles are on the shelf, of every scent together. `shelf` is an object whose keys are scents and whose values are counts, like `{ cedar: 4, fig: 0, amber: 12 }`. An empty shelf, `{}`, has `0`. The shelf object stays as it is.

Check calls `totalStock` with shelves of its own, an empty one included, and makes sure each shelf is unchanged afterwards.
nextSteps: Read the lesson's part on getting a list out of an object.
Get the counts of the shelf as a list.
Return the total and run the file.
hints: for...of goes through a list, not an object. Ask `Object` for a list first.
`Object.values(shelf)` is a list of the counts alone. From there it is the adding loop you know, or `reduce` with a starting value.
The function has the shape `let total = 0`, then `for (const count of Object.values(shelf)) { total = total + count }`, then `return total`.

tasks.title: Find the scents that ran out
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `soldOutScents(shelf)` return a list of the scents whose count is `0`, in the order they are in the shelf object. When none ran out, it returns an empty list. The shelf object stays as it is.

Check calls `soldOutScents` with shelves of its own, one with nothing sold out and an empty one included.
nextSteps: Go through the shelf's pairs of scent and count, and push the scent when its count is `0`.
Return the list and run the file: fig and sage should come back.
hints: You need both halves here: the count to ask about, and the scent to keep.
`Object.entries(shelf)` gives a list of pairs. Each pair is a small list: the key at index 0 and the value at index 1. `Object.keys` with brackets works too.
Inside `for (const entry of Object.entries(shelf))`, ask `if (entry[1] === 0)` and push `entry[0]`.

tasks.title: Make a price list
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `priceList(candles)` return a new object with one property per candle in the list: its key is the candle's `sku` and its value the candle's `priceCents`. An empty list gives `{}`. The list and its cards stay as they are.

With the catalogue at the top of the file, `priceList(catalogue)` gives `{ 'CED-200': 1800, 'FIG-350': 2400, 'AMB-200': 1900 }`.

Check calls `priceList` with lists of its own and makes sure each list is unchanged afterwards.
nextSteps: Go through the list of candles with `for...of`.
For each candle, add a property to your object, with the candle's sku as the key.
Return the object and run the file.
hints: Each candle in the list is an object, so `candle.sku` and `candle.priceCents` read its two values.
The key of the new property is not written in your code; it is the text inside `candle.sku`. That is a job for brackets with no quotes.
Inside the loop, `prices[candle.sku] = candle.priceCents`, with `const prices = {}` before it and `return prices` after.

tasks.title: What the stock is worth
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, first write a function of your own called `candleValue`, from the word `function` to its closing brace. It has one parameter, `candle`, and returns what the candles on that card are worth in cents: its `priceCents` times its `stock`. It only helps `stockValue`, so it stays off the `export` line.

Then make `stockValue(candles)` return what all the candles in the list are worth together, adding up what `candleValue` gives for each card. An empty list is worth `0`. The list and its cards stay as they are.

Check calls `candleValue` and `stockValue` with cards of its own, and reads your file for `candleValue` and the use of it inside `stockValue`.
nextSteps: Above `stockValue`, write `function candleValue(candle) {` and its closing `}` yourself.
Make it give back the card's price times its stock.
In `stockValue`, add up `candleValue` of every card, starting from 0.
Run the file: the last line is what the whole catalogue is worth.
hints: Two small jobs: one card, then the whole list. The first function does one card, the second calls it for each.
Adding up a list into one number is the job of a loop with a total, or of `reduce` with a starting value of 0.
`candleValue` is `return candle.priceCents * candle.stock`, and `stockValue` can be `return candles.reduce((total, candle) => total + candleValue(candle), 0)`.
